title: Install-Free Chromium Package Restore and Rendered Startup
criteria: From a clean checkout, `npm ci` restores dependencies using the committed `package-lock.json` and the project produces a desktop-web build without a native install step.
The project configuration and verification scope treat Chromium desktop web as the only approved platform for this increment; no cross-browser or real-device certification is introduced.
A clean Chromium desktop session can load the project package without installation and start the game.
Desktop web is the only approved PoC platform; no mobile or touch build is produced or required.
Chromium desktop is the primary verification target; responsive behavior is limited to desktop viewports and no cross-browser certification is required.

From a clean checkout, launch the approved Story's runnable slice using PixiJS v7 WebGL renderer with a custom TypeScript game loop; collision and layout logic implemented directly (no full arcade engine) and TypeScript. Commit package-lock.json and verify a clean dependency restore.
constraints: Engine and language: PixiJS v7 WebGL renderer with a custom TypeScript game loop.
Package manager evidence: package-lock.json generated or verified through npm; clean restore uses npm ci when the lockfile is committed.
Browser target: Chromium desktop web only; no mobile, touch, cross-browser certification, profiling, power-ups, or stress testing beyond stable observed playability.

Verification: Chromium startup and input behavior should be validated through the browser scenario runner; standalone dependency or build checks may use npm test or script-based verify commands rather than inline snippets.
Interaction criteria for running behavior require browser scenario evidence when implemented; documents and dependency checks may use build or script evidence.

Technical Director chose PixiJS v7 WebGL renderer with a custom TypeScript game loop; collision and layout logic implemented directly (no full arcade engine) with TypeScript and pixi.js, @pixi/filter-kawase-blur, @pixi/filter-glow, @pixi/filter-chromatic-aberration, tone, vite. Fixed constraints require a Chromium desktop web PoC with readable Breakout rules and a heavy juice/audio layer, but no mobile, cross-browser certification, profiling, or power-ups. PixiJS plus a custom loop is chosen because it gives WebGL compositing, particle containers, and custom GLSL filters for additive glow, bloom, chromatic shards, hit-stop, and screen shake while keeping gameplay logic simple enough for a one-screen Breakout. No external deadline or budget/time constraint has been recorded, so selection is by PoC merit rather than schedule. Canvas 2D was rejected as the main path because required bloom and shader-driven debris would be approximate and less maintainable. Phaser was rejected for this MVP despite faster scene and physics scaffolding because the required renderer juice exceeds default 2D conventions and would depend on plugin or renderer escape hatches. Raw WebGL or WebGPU was rejected because it gives the most visual control but adds too much boilerplate and maintenance for a PoC with one ball and fixed layouts. Tone.js is selected to prototype reactive chiptune layering and SFX without a full audio engine, accepting extra bundle size and Web Audio scheduling complexity as the main tradeoff. Accessibility is handled in the custom loop with reduced-motion, volume, remapping, audio-visual redundancy, and pause/restart; Pixi remains a desktop-web renderer dependency rather than a full game engine, keeping maintenance bounded.
